name: Point Charge in Three Dimensions
description: The static spacetime of a point electric charge in two dimensions of space and one of time, whose field fills the plane and curves spacetime everywhere, with a horizon on the circle $r = r_c$ beyond which $r$ is a time.
convention:
We keep factors of $c$ explicit. Einstein's equations read $G_{\mu
u} = kT_{\mu
u}$, with the stress tensor $T_{\mu
u} = (F_{\mu\alpha}F_
u{}^\alpha - 	frac{1}{4}g_{\mu
u}F_{\alpha eta}F^{\alpha eta})/2\pi$ of the charge's field $F = (Q/r)\,dr \wedge c\,dt$, whose strength is $E = Q/r$.
history: Spread over a plane, the electric field of a point charge $Q$ weakens only as $E = Q/r$, so slowly that its total energy is infinite [gott1986charged, deser1985]. With two dimensions of space, Einstein's equations leave spacetime flat wherever there is no matter, and the field of the charge is matter at every radius, so it curves the whole of spacetime [gott1986charged, cataldo1996]. The static, circularly symmetric spacetime of the charge has the line element $ds^2 = -\dfrac{kQ^2}{2\pi}\ln\left(\dfrac{r_c}{r}\right)c^2dt^2 + \dfrac{2\pi\,dr^2}{kQ^2\ln\left(\dfrac{r_c}{r}\right)} + r^2d\phi^2$, in which $r_c$ is a constant length and the circle of radius $r$ has circumference $2\pi r$ [gott1986charged, cataldo1996]. Here $k = 8\pi G/c^4$ couples matter to curvature, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions. The Ricci scalar, $R = kQ^2/2\pi r^2$, grows without bound at the charge.¶Stanley Deser and Pawel O. Mazur published this spacetime in May 1985, for a point charge with a mass [deser1985]. M. A. Melvin derived the electrostatic and magnetostatic solutions without a cosmological constant in January 1986, and J. Richard Gott III, Jonathan Z. Simon, and Mark Alpert published their electrically charged solution that October [garcia2009, melvin1986, gott1986charged]. Steven Carlip counts the three as independent discoveries of one metric [carlip1995]. Gott and Alpert had found in 1984 that a point mass in three dimensions sits at the apex of a cone whose angle deficit is proportional to the mass [gott1984]. Deser and Mazur found that the charge must vanish if the mechanical mass of the particle is large enough to close up space, and that no static solution holds two or more charges [deser1985].¶On the circle $r = r_c$ the logarithm vanishes and the spacetime has a horizon, which Gott, Simon, and Alpert likened to the inner horizon of the Reissner-Nordström black hole [gott1986charged]. Inside it the spacetime is static; outside it $r$ is a time [gott1986charged]. In their Kruskal extension, two static regions, each with a charge at $r = 0$, meet two dynamical ones [gott1986charged]. A spacelike slice across both static regions is "a football-shaped universe" with charge $Q$ at one end and $-Q$ at the other, and in the dynamical regions space is a cylinder, expanding in one and contracting in the other [gott1986charged]. For Deser and Mazur the circle is a Killing horizon, and the spacetime has no event horizon [deser1985]. Daisuke Ida proved in 2000 that matter obeying the dominant energy condition forbids a black hole in three dimensions with a positive cosmological constant, and noted that with no cosmological constant a Maxwell field rules out even degenerate apparent horizons [ida2000blackhole].¶Pujian Mao and Weicheng Zhao showed in 2024 that the horizon is cosmological, with every circle beyond $r_c$ trapped [mao2024]. Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Jorge Zanelli gave their black hole of 1992 an electric charge, and with the cosmological constant set to zero the charged solution is this metric [banados1992, carlip1995]. Jiří Podolský and Matúš Papajčík found every solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations in three dimensions with no charges or currents and any cosmological constant in 2022, and the static spacetime of a charge belongs to their expanding class of Robinson-Trautman spacetimes [podolsky2022]. Mao and Zhao also showed that with no cosmological constant the rotating charged solution differs from this one by a change of coordinates alone, so its rotation parameter describes no rotation of the source [mao2024].¶In two dimensions of space the electric field is a vector and the magnetic field a scalar, so no duality exchanges them, and Mauricio Cataldo and Patricio Salgado solved for each separately in 1996 [cataldo1996]. They showed that a magnetic solution follows from the static black hole of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli by exchanging the time with the angle and the electric charge with the magnetic one, each with a factor of $i$ [cataldo1996]. Gott, Simon, and Alpert turned to Kaluza-Klein theory, in which electromagnetic radiation in three dimensions is gravitational radiation in four [gott1986charged]. In the same way, gravity in three dimensions carries no waves, and so electromagnetism in one dimension of space and one of time carries none [gott1986charged].

related.text: A mass in three dimensions leaves space flat around it, a cone with its tip at the mass [gott1984]. Give the particle a charge and its field, spread over the plane, curves spacetime everywhere [gott1986charged].
Give the black hole of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli an electric charge and set its cosmological constant to zero, and it becomes this spacetime [banados1992, carlip1995].
The Reissner-Nordström black hole keeps its charge inside two horizons. Gott, Simon, and Alpert likened the one horizon at $r_c$ to the inner of the two [gott1986charged].

coordinates.name: Static

parameters.description: Coupling of Einstein's equations, $k = 8\pi G/c^4$ with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Electric charge of the source at $r = 0$
Radius of the horizon, a constant of integration independent of $Q$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $2\pi r$ the circumference of the circle of radius $r$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Coupling of Einstein's equations, $k = 8\pi G/c^4$ with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Electric charge of the source at $r = 0$
Radius of the horizon, a constant of integration independent of $Q$

coordinates.convention: We use Podolský and Papajčík's coordinates $(u, r, \phi)$, with $u$ the retarded time, $c\,du = c\,dt - 2\pi\,dr/(kQ^2\ln(r_c/r))$, constant along every outgoing light ray. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Coupling of Einstein's equations, $k = 8\pi G/c^4$ with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Electric charge of the source at $r = 0$
Radius of the horizon, a constant of integration independent of $Q$

coordinates.convention: We use Mao and Zhao's coordinates $(v, r, \phi)$, with $v$ the advanced time, $c\,dv = c\,dt + 2\pi\,dr/(kQ^2\ln(r_c/r))$, constant along every ingoing light ray. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.
